Every contradiction proof in this guide (Gale-Shapley stability, the cut property) has these same four moves.
(for a claim P(k) about every k = 1, 2, 3, ...):
Base case: show P(1) directly.
Inductive step: assume P(k - 1) (the inductive hypothesis) and show P(k).
Conclude P(k) holds for all k. Strong induction assumes P(1), ..., P(k - 1) all hold, which is equally valid.
Claim P(n): 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n + 1)/2 for every n >= 1.
Left side: 1. Right side: 1 times 2 / 2 = 1. Equal, so P(1) holds. (Always check the smallest case by plugging in numbers.)
Assume P(k - 1) holds for some k >= 2: 1 + 2 + ... + (k - 1) = (k - 1)k/2. (Write out exactly what you are allowed to assume. You may NOT assume P(k), the thing you are proving.)

1 + 2 + ... + k = [1 + 2 + ... + (k - 1)] + k. By the hypothesis this is (k - 1)k/2 + k = (k^2 - k + 2k)/2 = (k^2 + k)/2 = k(k + 1)/2. That is exactly P(k). (Split the new case into the old case plus one extra piece, then use the hypothesis on the old case.)
By induction, P(n) holds for every n >= 1.
The greedy-stays-ahead proof in Lesson 6 has exactly this shape, with "the r-th greedy pick finishes no later" in place of the sum formula.

Graph size facts
An undirected graph has at most n(n - 1)/2 edges (one per pair of nodes).
A connected graph has at least n - 1 edges. A tree has exactly n - 1 edges.
So for connected graphs, n - 1 <= m <= n^2, and log m is Theta(log n).
Lesson 1: Stable matching and Gale-Shapley
We want to pair n colleges with n students so that nobody has a reason to break the deal. Gale-Shapley does this in O(n^2) time, while trying all matchings would take Omega(n!).
Definitions to state exactly
a set M of (college, student) pairs where each college and each student appears in exactly one pair.
a pair (c, s) NOT in M where c prefers s to its current student AND s prefers c to her current college. Both conditions are required.
a matching with no unstable pairs.
Stable matchings always exist but are not always unique.

"a: 2, 1, 3" means college a likes student 2 best, then 1, then 3. "s prefers c to c'" just means c appears earlier on s's list than c'. A habit that saves time on exams: before tracing, circle each student's current partner on her list. Anything to the left of the circle is someone she would trade up to; anything to the right she would reject.
The algorithm in plain words

Free colleges take turns making offers, each going down its own preference list. A free student accepts any offer. A matched student swaps only if the new college is better (she "trades up"); the dropped college becomes free again.

paragraph.text: To sketch a matching problem, put colleges in a left column and students in a right column, and draw each offer as a line, numbered in order. Keep a running mark of who currently holds whom. At the end, the lines still standing are the matching.
Do stable matchings exist? Are they unique?
colleges a: 1 2 and b: 1 2; students 1: a b and 2: a b. M = {(a, 1), (b, 2)} is stable. M = {(a, 2), (b, 1)} is not: a and 1 both prefer each other to their partners.

colleges a: 1 2 and b: 2 1; students 1: b a and 2: a b. Both matchings are stable. In {(a, 1), (b, 2)} each college has its first choice, so no college wants to move. In {(a, 2), (b, 1)} each student has her first choice, so no student wants to move. So stable matchings can be non-unique.
Gale-Shapley proves one always exists, by always producing one.
Who proposes matters

Run Example B with colleges proposing: a offers to 1, b offers to 2, both accepted. Colleges get their first choices and students their last. With students proposing: 1 offers to b, 2 offers to a. Students get their first choices. In general the proposing side gets its best possible stable partner and the receiving side its worst. So students do better when they propose.
Why O(n^2), and why brute force is hopeless
Brute force would list all n! matchings and check each for stability, which takes Omega(n!) time. Gale-Shapley runs at most n^2 iterations, and each one takes O(1) time with these arrays:
next[c]: the position on c's list of the next student c will offer to.
current[s]: the college s currently holds, or none.
rank[s][c]: s's ranking of c, built once in O(n^2) time, so "does s prefer c to c'?" is a single comparison rank[s][c] < rank[s][c'].
A stack or queue of free colleges, so finding a free college is O(1).
Total: O(n^2) for setup plus O(n^2) iterations of O(1) work each, so O(n^2).

An array stores values at numbered positions, and reading position i takes the same constant time no matter how large the array is. A 2D array rank[s][c] is a table with a row per student and a column per college. Filling it costs n times n = n^2 steps, once. Without it, answering "does s prefer c to c'?" means scanning s's list, O(n) each time, which would make the whole algorithm O(n^3).
The two observations every proof uses
Once a student is matched she stays matched, and her partner only improves.
Each college offers to students in order of its preferences, never repeating.
The three proofs, walked through
Every iteration is a brand new (college, student) offer by F2. There are only n^2 such pairs, so at most n^2 iterations.

Suppose c and s are both unmatched at the end. By F1, s was never matched. The loop stopped with c free, so c must have offered to everyone, including s. But s was free then and would have accepted. Contradiction.

Suppose (c, s) is unstable: c is with s' but prefers s, and s is with c' but prefers c. Since c ranks s above s', by F2 c offered to s before s'. Whatever s did then, by F1 she only traded up afterward, so she must like her final c' at least as much as c. That contradicts s preferring c to c'.
Proof deep dive: stability, with the thinking shown
The three proofs above are what you write on the exam. Here is the same stability proof slowed down, showing how you would come up with it.
Show the final matching M has no unstable pair.
"No unstable pair" is a statement that something never happens. Those are almost always proved by contradiction: assume it does happen, then show the algorithm could not have produced that situation.

text.bold: Step 1: write down everything the assumption gives you.

paragraph.text: Suppose (c, s) is unstable in M. Unpack the definition into separate facts so you can use each one:
c is matched to some student s' in M (we already proved everyone is matched).
s is matched to some college c'.
c prefers s to s'.
s prefers c to c'.

text.bold: Step 2: ask what the algorithm did with these two.

paragraph.text: The algorithm only does two things: colleges offer, students accept or reject. So the natural question is: did c ever offer to s?
Fact 3 says s is earlier than s' on c's list.
c is matched to s', so c offered to s' at some point.
By F2, c offers in list order, so c must have offered to s before it got to s'. So yes, c offered to s.

text.bold: Step 3: follow s from that moment.

paragraph.text: When c offered, one of two things happened:
s rejected c. A student only rejects when she already holds someone she likes more. So at that moment she held a college better than c.
s accepted c, but c did not end up with her, so later she dropped c for a college she likes more.
Either way, at some moment s held a college she likes more than c.

text.bold: Step 4: carry that forward to the end.

paragraph.text: By F1, a student's partner only improves. So her final partner c' is at least as good as that college, which means s prefers c' to c.
Step 4 says s prefers c' to c. Fact 4 says s prefers c to c'. Both cannot be true, so our assumption was false: M has no unstable pair.

text.bold: See it on the worked example.

paragraph.text: Final M = {(a, 2), (b, 3), (c, 1)}. College a prefers 1 to its partner 2, so (a, 1) is the kind of pair the proof worries about. Did a offer to 1? Yes, in step 1 of the trace. What happened next? Student 1 traded up to c, whom she ranks above a. So 1 prefers her final partner c to a, and (a, 1) is not unstable, exactly as Steps 3 and 4 predict.
the four facts named; F2 used to show c offered to s; both cases (rejected, or accepted then dropped); F1 used to carry the improvement to the end; the contradiction stated explicitly.

Lesson 2: Big-O, Big-Omega, Big-Theta

We measure running time T(n) as a function of input size n, then ignore constant factors and lower-order terms so we can compare algorithms by growth rate. Binary search (about log n steps) beats linear search (n steps) no matter what the constants are.
The three definitions
Notation
Means
Definition (exists c > 0 and n0 >= 0 such that for all n >= n0)
T is O(f)
T grows at most as fast as f (upper bound)
T(n) <= c f(n)
T is Omega(f)
T grows at least as fast as f (lower bound)
T(n) >= c f(n)
T is Theta(f)
same growth rate (tight bound)
T is both O(f) and Omega(f)
Bounds need not be tight: 2n^2 + n + 2 is O(n^2), O(n^3), and O(2^n). That is why we need Omega and Theta to say two algorithms really differ.

text.bold: Refresher: how to read the big-O definition.

paragraph.text: Picture two curves, T(n) and c times f(n). The definition says: past some point n0, the curve c f(n) is a ceiling that T(n) never pokes above. You get to choose c (how high to scale the ceiling) and n0 (where you start checking). Small n do not matter, which is why n0 exists. Constant factors do not matter, which is why c exists. Big-Omega is the same picture with c f(n) as a floor instead.
Worked proof: big-O from the definition
Claim: T(n) = 2n^2 + n + 2 is O(n^2).
Bound every lower-order term by the top power, valid once n >= 1: n <= n^2 and 2 <= 2n^2.
So T(n) <= 2n^2 + n^2 + 2n^2 = 5n^2 for all n >= 1.
State the constants: c = 5, n0 = 1.
Proof deep dive: finding c and n0, scratch work vs write-up
Claim: T(n) = 3n^2 - 5n + 10 is O(n^2).
You want T(n) <= c n^2. Handle each term:
3n^2 is already a multiple of n^2. Keep it.
-5n is negative. Dropping a negative term only makes the expression bigger, so T(n) <= 3n^2 + 10 is safe.
10 is a constant. For n >= 1, n^2 >= 1, so 10 <= 10n^2.
Add up: T(n) <= 3n^2 + 10n^2 = 13n^2 when n >= 1.
Notice the write-up is a single chain of inequalities, each step justified by something simple, ending with the named constants. That is the format graders want.
Claim: n^2 is not O(n).
Suppose for contradiction there are constants c and n0 with n^2 <= c n for all n >= n0.
Divide both sides by n (positive): n <= c for all n >= n0.
Pick n = max(n0, c + 1). It is at least n0, but it is bigger than c. That breaks step 2.
Contradiction, so no such c and n0 exist.
The pattern: assume the constants exist, simplify to "something growing <= a constant", then pick an n big enough to break it.
Worked proof: big-Omega from the definition
Claim: n - 10 is Omega(n).
We want n - 10 >= c n. Try c = 1/2: we need n - 10 >= n/2, which means n/2 >= 10, so n >= 20.
State the constants: c = 1/2, n0 = 20. (Any c < 1 works with a large enough n0; c = 1 or more never works.)
To prove a lower bound, you throw away positive terms or show negative terms are small compared to the main term.

text.bold: Refresher: moving inequalities in the safe direction.

paragraph.text: For an upper bound (proving T <= something), you may only make the right side bigger: drop negative terms, or replace a term with a larger one (for n >= 1: 1 <= n <= n^2 <= n^3). For a lower bound (proving T >= something), you may only make the right side smaller: drop positive terms, or replace a subtracted term with a larger subtracted term (for n >= 1: -2n^2 >= -2n^3). Mixing the directions up is the most common algebra error on these proofs.
Properties you can use as shortcuts
f is O(g) and g is O(h) imply f is O(h). Proof: multiply the constants (c'' = c c') and take n0'' = max(n0, n0').
if f is O(g), then f + g is Theta(g). So you drop lower-order terms, and a polynomial is Theta of its highest-degree term.
log n is O(n^d) for every d > 0, and n^d is O(r^n) for every r > 1. Logs lose to polynomials; polynomials lose to exponentials.
log_a n = (log_a b) log_b n, a constant factor. Write log n, meaning base 2.
Worked comparison: n (log n)^3 vs n^(4/3)
Divide both by n: (log n)^3 vs n^(1/3).
Take the cube root of both: log n vs n^(1/9).
log n is O(n^(1/9)) by the hierarchy, so n (log n)^3 is O(n^(4/3)).
Applying the same monotone operation (divide, root, log) to both sides keeps the comparison honest.
Counting loops
Nested independent loops multiply: two loops of n each give Theta(n^2); three give Theta(n^3).
Dependent loops (j from i to n) sum: 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n + 1)/2, which is Theta(n^2).
ignore iterations where i > n/2 or j < n/2. The rest still run at least (n/2)(n/2) = n^2/4 times, so Omega(n^2).
A loop that only runs under a condition (if i == 1) runs once in total, not n times.
A variable that doubles each step (j = 2j until n) runs about log n times.

text.bold: Refresher: why doubling gives log n.

paragraph.text: Trace j = 1, 2, 4, 8, ... while j < n with n = 16: j takes the values 1, 2, 4, 8 and then becomes 16, which stops the loop. That is 4 iterations, and log 16 = 4. In general, after k doublings j = 2^k, and the loop stops once 2^k >= n, that is once k >= log n. Halving (i = n, n/2, n/4, ...) is the same count in reverse.
Efficiency
An algorithm is
if it runs in polynomial time, O(n^d) for some constant d. n log n, 0.01n^2, and 20n^2 + 2n + 3 are polynomial; 2^n, 3^n, and n! are not.
Correct phrasing: "the running time is O(n^3)" or "T(n) is O(n^3)". Avoid "O(n^3) is the running time", since there are many valid upper bounds.

Suppose f is O(g). Must g be O(f)?

(1) Both; bounds need not be tight. (2) It depends: f = n, g = n works both ways, but f = n, g = n^2 does not. (3) 2n characters, Theta(n).

Find c and n0 showing 7n^2 - 3n is Omega(n^2).
Prove n^3 is not O(n^2).

For large n, which is bigger: n^10 or 2^n? n or (log n)^5?

R2.4: 3n, which is Theta(n). The inner loop has a fixed length, so it is a constant factor.

paragraph.text: True or false: 2^(2n) is O(2^n).

P2.1: Upper: for n >= 1, 7 <= 7n^3 and -2n^2 <= 0, so the expression is at most 5n^3 + 7n^3 = 12n^3 (c = 12, n0 = 1). Lower: for n >= 1, 2n^2 <= 2n^3 and +7 > 0, so the expression is at least 5n^3 - 2n^3 = 3n^3 (c = 3, n0 = 1). Both together give Theta(n^3).

Lesson 3: Graphs and breadth-first search

A graph G = (V, E) models anything with connections: roads, friendships, web links, prerequisites. We always write n = |V| and m = |E|. BFS explores outward from a start node s like an expanding wave, one distance at a time, in Theta(m + n) time.
Vocabulary to state exactly
e = (u, v): u and v are neighbors (adjacent, endpoints of e); e is incident to u and v.
a sequence v1, ..., vk where each consecutive pair is joined by an edge. Repeats are allowed.
a path with all vertices distinct.
a path with v1 = vk, the first k - 1 nodes distinct, and k > 3.
from u to v: the minimum number of edges on a u to v path.
a path exists between every pair of nodes.
a maximal set of nodes with a path between every pair (adding any other node breaks that).
a connected graph with no cycles. A
orients every edge away from a chosen root r; the parent of v is its predecessor on the path from r.
V is just a list of nodes with no repeats. An undirected edge {u, v} is an unordered pair, so (u, v) and (v, u) are the same edge. The
of a node is how many edges touch it. Degree comes up constantly: BFS and DFS cost is really "sum of degrees", and that sum is always 2m.
How to sketch a graph from an edge list (fast)
Exams hand you graphs as lists. A good sketch takes about a minute once you have a method, and it makes every later step (BFS, cycles, bipartite) visible. The method is BFS done by hand.
Go through the edge list once and add a mark next to each endpoint. Sum the marks; it must equal 2m. If it does not, you misread an edge.
Use the one the problem names. If none, use a high-degree node: hubs make good roots.

Key fact: Li is exactly the set of nodes at distance i from s. So t is reachable from s if and only if t appears in some layer.

text.bold: Why layers equal distances (proof by induction on i).

paragraph.text: Let Di be the set of nodes at distance exactly i. Claim: Li = Di for every i. Base: L0 = {s} = D0. Step: assume Lj = Dj for all j <= i.

If v is in D(i+1): the node just before v on a shortest path is at distance i, so it is in Li and has an edge to v. v is not in any earlier layer, since those hold only nodes at distance <= i. So v is in L(i+1).
If v is in L(i+1): v has an edge to a node at distance i, so its distance is at most i + 1. It is in no earlier layer Lj = Dj, so its distance is not <= i. So its distance is exactly i + 1.

paragraph.text: When DFS(1) calls DFS(2), DFS(1) is paused, not finished. The computer keeps a stack of paused calls; the newest call runs, and when it returns, the one below it resumes exactly where it stopped. "Backtracking" is just this: returning to the paused call below.

Claim: DFS non-tree edges lead to ancestors
Let (x, y) be an edge not in T, with x explored first.
When DFS(x) starts, y is not explored yet.
At some point DFS(x) examines edge (x, y). If y were still unexplored, we would add (x, y) to T. It is not in T, so y is explored by then.

BFS layers do more than measure distance. Coloring even layers red and odd layers blue tests bipartiteness, and a variant of "repeatedly remove a node with nothing pointing at it" orders a dependency graph.
Bipartite graphs
G is
if V splits into X and Y with every edge having one end in each (color nodes red and blue so no edge joins two of the same color). Stable matching's college-student graph is bipartite. Any
is not: going around it alternates colors, and an odd length makes the last node clash with the first.
run BFS from any node. If some edge joins two nodes in the same layer, output "not bipartite". Otherwise output X = even layers, Y = odd layers.
If it says bipartite: every BFS edge joins the same or adjacent layers. No same-layer edges means every edge joins adjacent layers, one even and one odd.

If it says not bipartite: take the edge (x, y) inside layer j. Let z, in layer i, be the least common ancestor of x and y in the BFS tree. Walk z down to x, cross (x, y), walk y back up to z. That cycle has length (j - i) + 1 + (j - i) = 2(j - i) + 1, which is odd, so G is not bipartite.

In a rooted tree, an ancestor of x is any node on the path from the root down to x (its parent, grandparent, and so on). The least common ancestor of x and y is the deepest node that is an ancestor of both: walk both up toward the root, and the first node where the two walks meet is it. The two walks down from it to x and to y share no nodes other than z, which is why gluing them with the edge (x, y) gives a genuine cycle.

the 5-cycle a, b, c, d, e, a. BFS from a: L0 = {a}, L1 = {b, e}, L2 = {c, d}. Edge (c, d) lies inside L2. The parents are b and e, whose parent is a, so z = a with i = 0 and j = 2. The cycle a, b, c, d, e, a has length 2(2 - 0) + 1 = 5.

paragraph.text: The walk from z = a down to c uses j - i = 2 edges (a-b, b-c). The edge c-d is 1 more. The walk from d back up to a uses another j - i = 2 edges (d-e, e-a). Total 2(j - i) + 1 = 5. The same count works for any same-layer edge, because both endpoints sit exactly j - i levels below z: the two halves always match, and the extra 1 makes the total odd. That odd cycle is the reason no 2-coloring can exist, so the algorithm is right to say "not bipartite".
G is bipartite if and only if it has no odd cycle. The algorithm proves the hard direction.

paragraph.text: "G is a DAG iff G has a topological ordering" is two claims. The first bullet proves "ordering implies DAG" in its contrapositive form, "has a cycle implies no ordering", which is logically the same statement and easier here. The contrapositive of "A implies B" is "not B implies not A"; they are always equivalent. (The converse "B implies A" is NOT equivalent, which is why both directions need their own proof.)

codeBlock.text: topo-sort(G): while nodes remain find a node v with no incoming edges place v next; delete v and its outgoing edges

paragraph.text: It can be implemented in O(m + n) by keeping each node's count of remaining incoming edges and a list of nodes whose count is 0.

text.bold: Step by step: the O(m + n) version.

paragraph.text: "Find a node with no incoming edges" would cost O(n) each time if you searched, making the algorithm O(n^2). Instead:
Count each node's incoming edges once by scanning every edge: O(m + n). Call it count(v).
Put every node with count 0 into a list S.
Repeatedly remove any node v from S and place it next in the order.
For each edge v to w, subtract 1 from count(w). If it hits 0, add w to S.

Lesson 7: Minimizing lateness and the exchange argument

Do your assignments in order of due date. Proving that is optimal teaches the second big greedy proof technique: take any optimal solution and transform it, step by step, into the greedy one without making it worse.
Formulation
Job j has length t(j) and deadline d(j). The algorithm picks start times s(j); finish f(j) = s(j) + t(j).
Lateness of j: 0 if f(j) <= d(j), otherwise f(j) - d(j).

lateness L over all jobs.

Two facts used in the proof

EDF schedules differ only in the order of equal-deadline jobs, which sit in one consecutive block. The block's last job has the largest lateness among them, and its finish time does not depend on the order inside the block. So all EDF schedules have the same L.
in schedule O, i comes before j but d(j) < d(i) (j "should" go first). If O has any inversion, it has a
one, with i immediately before j: walking from i to j, deadlines would otherwise never decrease.
Why the obvious proof fails
"Suppose EDF is not optimal; swap an inversion in the optimal O to get something better; contradiction." The swap only gives something
, possibly equally good, so there is no contradiction.
The correct exchange argument
Take any optimal O different from A. Show you can change it to O' that is (1) still optimal and (2) closer to A by a measurable amount. Repeat until you reach A.
O has a consecutive inversion: i right before j with d(j) <= d(i). Swap them to get O'.
O' has exactly one fewer inversion.
Lateness does not go up:
Every other job finishes at the same time, so its lateness is unchanged.
j now finishes earlier, so its lateness can only drop.
i now finishes where j used to, at f(j). Its new lateness is f(j) - d(i) <= f(j) - d(j), which is j's old lateness, because d(j) <= d(i).
So max lateness of O' <= that of O, and O' is still optimal.

There are at most n(n - 1)/2 inversions, so after finitely many swaps we reach an optimal schedule with no inversions. That is an EDF schedule, and all EDF schedules share the same L. So EDF is optimal.

Lesson 8: Shortest paths and Dijkstra's algorithm

BFS finds shortest paths when every edge counts as 1. Dijkstra generalizes it to nonnegative edge lengths by tracking the "arrival time" of a wave spreading out from s, always settling the closest unsettled node next.
Formulation

Directed graph with lengths l(e) >= 0. The length of a path is the sum of its edge lengths. d(v) is the length of the shortest s to v path. Goal: d(v) for every v at once (the work for one target already computes the rest).

Each edge now has a direction (u to v can be used only from u toward v) and a number, its length or weight. On a sketch, draw arrows and write each length beside its arrow. Starting every tentative distance at infinity is a trick that means "no path found yet": any real path length is smaller, so the first path found always replaces it.
Where it comes from

Replace an edge of integer length l with a chain of l unit edges and run BFS: layer i is exactly the set of nodes at distance i. That works but costs O(n + C m) where C is the longest edge, terrible when C is 1000 or a billion, because BFS wastes time walking through the dummy nodes. Dijkstra skips straight to the next real node the wave will hit.
The algorithm
d'(v): tentative arrival time, the best path found so far.
d(v): final shortest distance, set when v is extracted.

Lesson 9: Minimum spanning trees, cut property, Kruskal, Prim, union-find
Connect every node as cheaply as possible. One theorem, the cut property, tells you an edge is "safe" to include, and two different greedy algorithms are just two ways of applying it.
Formulation

Undirected connected graph, edge costs c(e) > 0, assumed distinct for now. Find T, a subset of E, with (V, T) connected and total cost minimal. The answer is always a spanning tree: if it had a cycle, dropping any cycle edge keeps it connected and lowers the cost.

text.bold: Refresher: three tree facts used in every MST proof.

paragraph.text: (1) A tree on n nodes has exactly n - 1 edges. (2) Adding any one new edge to a tree creates exactly one cycle: the new edge plus the tree path between its endpoints. (3) Removing any one edge from a tree splits it into exactly two pieces. The cut property's swap uses (2) to create a cycle and then removes an edge on that cycle, which by (3) applied to the cycle keeps everything connected.
Cuts
A
splits the nodes into two nonempty sets S and V - S.
An edge
the cut if it has one endpoint on each side. The crossing edges form the
Cut property (the key theorem)
If e is the cheapest edge crossing some cut, then e is in every MST.
suppose MST T does not contain e = (v, w), with v in S and w outside.
T is connected, so it has a path from v to w. That path starts in S and ends outside, so it has a first edge e' crossing the cut.
Let T' = T + e - e'. It is still connected (any route that used e' can detour through e) and still acyclic (adding e makes exactly one cycle, which contains e', and removing e' breaks it).
cost(T') = cost(T) - c(e') + c(e) < cost(T), since e is the cheapest crossing edge. Contradiction.
"swap e for any crossing edge f of T." If f is not on T's path from v to w, then T - f + e can be disconnected and contain a cycle. You must pick e' on that path.

Format 3: counting topological orderings

Go step by step. At each step, list the nodes with no remaining incoming edges; each choice is a branch. Count the leaves of that branching. When the DAG is two separate chains between a common first and last node, there is a shortcut: chains with p and q nodes interleave in C(p + q, p) ways, because you only choose which of the p + q middle positions the first chain takes.
C(a, b) = a! / (b! (a - b)!) counts the ways to pick b positions out of a. C(3, 1) = 3, C(5, 2) = 10, C(6, 3) = 20.

DAG with edges s to x, x to y, y to t, s to z, z to t. s must be first and t last. In between, the chain x, y and the single node z interleave: z goes before x, between x and y, or after y. That is C(3, 1) = 3 orderings: s, z, x, y, t; s, x, z, y, t; s, x, y, z, t.

text.bold: "Must u come before w in every ordering?"

paragraph.text: Yes exactly when there is a directed path from u to w. With no path either way, some ordering puts each one first. Above, x always precedes t (path x, y, t), but z and y appear in both orders.
Format 4: how many traversal starts?

In a DAG, the fewest traversal starts that discover every node equals the number of sources (nodes with no incoming edges). In graph H from the Lesson 5 practice, the sources are S and T, so 2 starts.
Every source must be a start: nothing points into it, so no search from elsewhere finds it.

Starting at every source finds everything: from any node, walk backward along incoming edges. In a DAG the walk cannot repeat a node, so it stops within n steps at a node with no incoming edges, a source. Reverse that walk to get a path from a source to the node.
Time: count incoming edges in O(m + n); all the traversals together explore each node and edge once, O(m + n).

When a question gives a hint such as "what would you do on a single path?", actually work that tiny case by hand, trying different start orders, before generalizing. The pattern you see there is usually the whole answer.
Format 5: three Big-O proof patterns
Claim: 2^n is O(n!).
Write both as products: 2^n = 2 times 2 times ... times 2 (n factors); n! = 1 times 2 times 3 times ... times n.
Line the factors up. In the first position, 2 beats 1. In every later position k, the factorial's factor k is at least 2.
So n! = 1 times (2 times 3 times ... times n) >= 1 times 2^(n - 1).
Multiply by 2: 2 times n! >= 2^n for all n >= 1. Constants c = 2, n0 = 1.
The constant c absorbs the few early factors where the exponential is ahead.
Claim: n log n is not O(n). Suppose n log n <= c n for all n >= n0. Divide by n: log n <= c for all n >= n0. Take n = max(n0, 2^(c + 1)); then log n >= c + 1 > c. Contradiction.
Claim: if g1 is O(h1) and g2 is O(h2), then g1 + g2 is O(h1 + h2).
Write each definition with its own constants: g1(n) <= c1 h1(n) for n >= n1, and g2(n) <= c2 h2(n) for n >= n2.
Work where both hold: n >= max(n1, n2).
Combine: g1 + g2 <= c1 h1 + c2 h2 <= max(c1, c2) times (h1 + h2) (functions here are nonnegative).
Name the constants: c = max(c1, c2), n0 = max(n1, n2).
The same four-step recipe proves other combination rules; only step 3 changes.

Test the claim on n = 2 instances first (Examples A and B in Lesson 1 are the usual suspects). If it seems true, explain with F1 and F2 and what the algorithm does. If false, give a complete counterexample: both sides' preference lists, plus the matching and the unstable pair or second stable matching that breaks the claim.

"If every college ranks a different student first, college-proposing Gale-Shapley gives every college its first choice." In the first round every college offers to its own top student. Those students are all different, so each is free and accepts. No college is ever rejected or dropped, so the algorithm stops after n offers with every college holding its first choice.

"Gale-Shapley always gives every student her first choice." Counterexample, Example B: colleges a: 1 2, b: 2 1; students 1: b a, 2: a b. Colleges propose: a offers to 1 and b offers to 2, both accepted, done. Student 1 ends with a, her second choice.
Format 7: graphs where every node has degree 2

If every node has exactly two neighbors, every connected component is a cycle. Why: start anywhere and walk without reusing an edge. Each node you arrive at has exactly one unused edge left, so you keep going until you return to the start, which closes a cycle; every node on it has used both its edges, so nothing else attaches. Such a graph is bipartite exactly when every one of its cycles has even length.
The cycle lengths add up to 7, an odd number, so at least one cycle is odd. Every 2-regular graph on 7 nodes is therefore NOT bipartite, connected or not.

Common mistakes that cost points
Calling (c, s) unstable when only one side prefers the other. Both must.
Big-O constants that depend on n ("c = n"). c and n0 must be fixed numbers.
Saying "O(n^3) is the running time". Say the running time is O(n^3), and use Theta when you mean tight.
Believing a greedy rule because it worked on examples. One counterexample kills a rule; only a proof saves it.
In an exchange argument, claiming the swap makes the solution strictly better. It only needs to be no worse and one step closer.
In the cut property proof, swapping out any crossing edge. It must be the crossing edge on T's path between e's endpoints.
Running Dijkstra with negative edges, or forgetting where the proof uses nonnegative lengths.
Thinking BFS layers depend on exploration order. Layers are distances; only the tree can change.
In induction, skipping the base case or using the claim for k to prove the claim for k.
Mixing up Prim and Dijkstra keys: Prim uses the single edge cost c(v, w), Dijkstra uses the path length d(v) + l(v, w).

Let A be shortest-first. Take any optimal O different from A. Then O has adjacent jobs i then j with t(i) > t(j). Swap them to get O'. Every other job finishes at the same time. Before the swap, with start time S, the pair contributes (S + t(i)) + (S + t(i) + t(j)). After, it contributes (S + t(j)) + (S + t(j) + t(i)). The difference is t(i) - t(j) > 0, so O' is strictly better, contradicting O being optimal. (Here the swap is strictly better because the lengths differ; jobs of equal length can be ordered either way without changing the sum.) So an optimal schedule has no such pair, which means it is in shortest-first order, and A is optimal.
